title: Budgeting from First Principles
subject: Financial Literacy
developmentNotes: Students need realistic but privacy-safe money reasoning, using fictional numbers rather than personal finances.
learningObjective: Students will create a simple budget by reasoning from income, needs, wants, savings, and tradeoffs.
essentialQuestion: How can first-principles thinking help people make better money decisions?

vocabularyTerms.definition: A plan for how money will be used.
Something required for basic responsibility, safety, or health.
Giving up one option to choose another.

hook.content: You have $100 for the week. Food, transportation, savings, and entertainment all compete for the same money.
hook.studentAction: Decide what must be paid first and explain why.
hook.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
hook.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

learningGoal.content: I can build a simple budget from first principles by identifying income, needs, wants, savings, and tradeoffs.
learningGoal.studentAction: Restate budget as a plan for limited money.
learningGoal.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
learningGoal.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

miniTeach.content: A budget starts with income. Then subtract needs, choose savings, and decide how much is left for wants. Every choice has an opportunity cost.
miniTeach.studentAction: Classify expenses as needs, wants, or savings.
miniTeach.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
miniTeach.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

firstPrinciplesBreakdown.content: Break budgeting down: How much money comes in? What must be paid? What future goal matters? What choices remain?
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.studentAction: Fill in income, fixed needs, variable choices, savings goal.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
firstPrinciplesBreakdown.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

workedExample.content: Income $100. Needs: bus $20, lunch $30. Savings $10. Wants budget: $40. If entertainment costs $50, something must change.
workedExample.studentAction: Calculate remaining money and identify the tradeoff.
workedExample.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
workedExample.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

guidedPractice.content: Build a $75 weekend budget with required transportation and food costs.
guidedPractice.studentAction: Subtract needs, set savings, choose wants.
guidedPractice.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
successCriteria: Creates a balanced budget that does not overspend.
guidedPractice.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

criticalThinkingCheckpoint.content: Is a cheap option always the best option? Consider quality, safety, time, and goals.
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.studentAction: Compare two spending choices using constraints.
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
successCriteria: Identifies at least one tradeoff beyond price.
criticalThinkingCheckpoint.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

evidenceBasedReasoningTask.content: Claim: This budget works. Evidence: total expenses are less than or equal to income. Reasoning: A budget cannot spend more than it has.
evidenceBasedReasoningTask.studentAction: Use numbers as evidence to defend a budget.
evidenceBasedReasoningTask.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
evidenceBasedReasoningTask.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

interpretationOrDiscussionTask.content: Discussion frame: 'I would prioritize ___ because ___. The tradeoff is ___.'
interpretationOrDiscussionTask.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
interpretationOrDiscussionTask.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

activePractice.content: Create a first-principles budget for a fictional student earning $120.
activePractice.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
successCriteria: Budget balances and includes a savings choice.
activePractice.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

retrievalCheck.content: Without looking, name the four budget building blocks.
retrievalCheck.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
retrievalCheck.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

feedback.content: Feedback checks arithmetic, category choices, and reasoning about tradeoffs.
feedback.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
successCriteria: Corrects the budget and explains the tradeoff.
feedback.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

reflection.content: What spending choice would be hardest for you to control, and what rule could help?
reflection.studentAction: Write one personal budgeting rule without sharing private financial data.
reflection.teacherOrAppAction: Guide with age-appropriate prompts, immediate feedback, and accessibility support.
successCriteria: Creates a general rule without sensitive personal disclosure.
reflection.cognitiveLoadNotes: Keep the task focused, reduce unnecessary text, and show examples before independent work.

quiz.question: What is income?
quiz.explanation: A budget starts with money available.

quiz.question: Which is usually a need?
quiz.explanation: Needs are expenses required for basic responsibilities or safety.

quiz.question: If income is $100 and needs cost $60, how much remains before savings or wants?
What is a tradeoff?
choices: Giving up one option to choose another
quiz.correctAnswer: Giving up one option to choose another

quiz.question: A budget spends $125 with income of $100. What is wrong?
quiz.explanation: A balanced budget cannot spend more than income.

quiz.question: Which evidence best proves a budget works?
choices: Total expenses are less than or equal to income
quiz.correctAnswer: Total expenses are less than or equal to income
quiz.explanation: Numbers provide evidence that the budget balances.

quiz.question: Build a budget: income $80, needs $50, savings $10. How much is left for wants?
quiz.scoringNotes: Award full credit for accurate reasoning with relevant evidence; partial credit for incomplete but coherent thinking.

quiz.question: Explain why savings can be treated like a planned category.
quiz.correctAnswer: Savings supports a future goal, so it should be planned before spending all remaining money on wants.
quiz.explanation: Savings becomes stronger when it is intentional.
quiz.scoringNotes: Award full credit for accurate reasoning with relevant evidence; partial credit for incomplete but coherent thinking.

quiz.question: Use CER to defend a balanced budget.
quiz.correctAnswer: Claim: The budget works. Evidence: Expenses add to the same amount or less than income. Reasoning: The plan does not overspend.
quiz.explanation: Budget reasoning should use numerical evidence.
quiz.scoringNotes: Award full credit for accurate reasoning with relevant evidence; partial credit for incomplete but coherent thinking.

quiz.question: Name one tradeoff in choosing a cheaper option.
quiz.correctAnswer: A cheaper option may save money but could take more time or be lower quality.
quiz.scoringNotes: Award full credit for accurate reasoning with relevant evidence; partial credit for incomplete but coherent thinking.

quiz.question: Explain one important idea from budgeting from first principles using your own words.
quiz.correctAnswer: A strong answer accurately explains budgeting from first principles and includes a reason or example.
quiz.explanation: This checks whether the student can explain budgeting from first principles, not just recognize it.
quiz.scoringNotes: Look for accurate concept, reasoning, and a relevant example.

reteachPath.misconception: Student guesses budgets without subtracting income and expenses step by step.
reteachPath.simpleExplanation: A budget is math plus priorities. Start with income, subtract needs, choose savings, then decide wants.
reteachPath.exitCriteria: Student builds a budget that balances and explains one tradeoff with numbers.

tasks: Design two budgets with different priorities and compare the tradeoffs.
Create a savings plan for a fictional $200 goal.
Analyze an overspending budget and propose three fixes.
challengePath.extensionRule: Unlock when budget calculations and tradeoff reasoning are both strong.

successCriteria: I can separate needs, wants, income, and fixed or flexible costs.
I can build a balanced budget from constraints.
I can explain tradeoffs instead of hiding them.
I can revise a budget when conditions change.

knowledge: A budget is a plan for allocating limited resources toward goals.
capability: Build and test a constrained budget.
reasoning: Use first principles and tradeoffs to justify spending choices.
retention: Recall budget categories and constraint checks after a delay.
transfer: Apply budgeting to a new project, event, or personal scenario without entering private financial data.

phaseModules.title: Meet the constraint
phaseModules.studentAction: Inspect a fictional budget goal and identify the limited resources and priorities.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name the goal and constraint.

phaseModules.title: Watch a budget balance
phaseModules.studentAction: Follow a model that allocates income, fixed costs, flexible costs, savings, and buffer.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can explain each category's job.

phaseModules.title: Find the tradeoffs
phaseModules.studentAction: Sort costs and test what happens when one category changes.
phaseModules.successCheck: I can name who or what is affected by a tradeoff.

phaseModules.title: Build the budget
phaseModules.studentAction: Use fictional amounts to create a balanced plan and check the total.
phaseModules.successCheck: Income, costs, and goal allocations reconcile.

phaseModules.title: Defend the choice
phaseModules.studentAction: Compare two balanced budgets and defend one using constraints and priorities.
phaseModules.successCheck: I explain tradeoffs rather than calling one choice universally best.

phaseModules.title: Solve a new scenario
phaseModules.studentAction: Build and explain a budget for a new classroom-safe project.
phaseModules.successCheck: The plan is balanced and justified.

phaseModules.title: Retrieve the budget test
phaseModules.studentAction: Recall goal, resources, categories, constraints, and tradeoffs after a delay.

phaseModules.title: Plan a project
phaseModules.studentAction: Apply the method to a fictional trip, event, club, or capstone budget.
phaseModules.successCheck: The method transfers without private data.

phaseModules.title: Revise after a change
phaseModules.studentAction: Adjust the plan when a cost changes and explain the new tradeoff.
phaseModules.successCheck: My revision protects the stated goal.

proofTasks.prompt: Define income, fixed cost, flexible cost, savings, and tradeoff.
Explain why a balanced budget still requires tradeoffs.
Build a balanced fictional budget from constraints.
Retrieve the budget check after a delay.
Apply the method to a new fictional project.

feedbackRules.result: The learner mixes fixed, flexible, goal, and buffer costs.
feedbackRules.hint: Ask whether the amount is required, changeable, or chosen for a goal.

feedbackRules.result: The plan does not reconcile to the available resources.
feedbackRules.hint: Add every allocation and compare it with total income.

reteachPaths.action: Sort fictional expenses by whether they are fixed, flexible, goal-based, or buffer.

prerequisiteRepairPaths.trigger: The learner cannot add or compare the fictional amounts.
prerequisiteRepairPaths.action: Repair decimal operations with small classroom-safe totals.

challengePaths.trigger: The learner builds a balanced plan.
challengePaths.action: Add a changed cost and defend a revision that protects the goal.

visualSupports.title: Budget control panel
visualSupports.description: A fictional resource pool flows into goals, costs, savings, and buffer.
visualSupports.altText: A labeled resource pool connects to budget categories.

visualSupports.title: Balance and tradeoff map
visualSupports.description: A diagram shows how allocations must balance while priorities compete.
visualSupports.altText: Arrows connect resources to categories and tradeoffs.

visualSupports.title: Budget builder
visualSupports.description: The learner adjusts fictional amounts and sees a balance check update.
visualSupports.altText: Labeled fictional amounts update a text balance result.

visualSupports.title: Balanced is not perfect
visualSupports.description: A comparison shows a balanced plan that still requires a tradeoff.
visualSupports.altText: A balanced plan is contrasted with the idea that one choice is universally best.

visualSupports.title: Budget check cue
visualSupports.description: A cue asks what is available, required, flexible, goal-based, and changed.
visualSupports.altText: Five questions cue the budget reasoning process.

parentTeacherNotes: Use fictional budgets only. Ask the student to explain priorities generally, not reveal family finances.
safetyNotes: Do not ask for real family income or expenses
implementationNotes: Use this lesson to test Problem-Solving Lab, Systems Mapper, and Life Skills content.
